children.text: Known as the highest peak on Cebu Island at an elevation of about
, just
20–30 minutes
climb from the jump-off point reveals a landscape of sharp limestone peaks rippling like waves. It's popular for sunrise hikes, camping, and a traverse trek down to Kawasan Falls.
Osmeña Peak rises in the inland south of Cebu Island, on the border between Barangay Mantalongon of the municipality of Dalaguete and Badian. At an elevation of about

, it's commonly introduced as 'Cebu's highest peak,' named after Sergio Osmeña, president during the Philippine Commonwealth era. Mountains usually bring to mind a long climbing trail, but here the jump-off point itself is a plateau several hundred meters above sea level, so it's a 'great value mountain' where the summit is just
20–30 minutes
on foot.

Standing at the summit, you immediately understand why Osmeña Peak is special. Grass-covered limestone peaks rise sharply like sawteeth, layered one after another, forming a unique terrain like a sharpened version of Bohol's Chocolate Hills. On clear days, you can see the mountain ranges of Negros Island across the Tañon Strait to the west, and the sea toward the Bohol Sea to the east, taking in the ocean on both sides of the island at once.

The Mantalongon area is an agricultural zone known as 'Cebu's vegetable basket,' thanks to its cool highland climate. Terraced fields of cabbage, tomato, and carrot spread out on either side of the trail, showing a landscape completely different from other Philippine beach destinations. Temperatures run more than 5°C lower than the coast, cool enough to feel chilly at dawn.

It's a short route that even hiking beginners and families can manage without strain, while also letting you raise the difficulty with sunrise camping or a long-distance traverse trek all the way down to Kawasan Falls. Fitting in a day between southern Cebu's coastal itinerary (Moalboal, Oslob, Kawasan) brings a balance of mountain and sea to your trip.

A tourist information board at the summit says the peak is in Barangay Patong in Badian and is 1,013m high. That is why, although many people climb from Mantalongon on the Dalaguete side, it also appears on Badian's maps and notices. Sources give the height anywhere from 1,013m to the 1,070m range, so think of it as 'roughly 1,000m.' The old name is said to have been 'Tan-awan,' meaning a lookout in Cebuano, and one story has it that the current name came about because President Osmeña often visited on horseback with his family. Casino Peak (Lugsangan Peak) and Kandungaw Peak are close by within Mantalongon, so many travelers combine them as the 'Mantalongon three peaks.'

blocks.title: Watch the sunrise from the summit

children.text: Set off from the jump-off around
and watch the sun rise from the summit. On days when a sea of clouds settles between the peaks, it's truly a spectacular view.

Shoot from the rocks near the summit toward the direction where the sharp peaks overlap, and you'll get Osmeña Peak's signature photo. The depth looks best when the morning light comes in at an angle.
Pitch a tent on the flat clearing below the summit and enjoy the night sky's stars together with the dawn sunrise. Rent a tent locally or bring your own.
This is a long-distance route that goes from Osmeña Peak through mountain trails, villages, and valleys, walking down from Mantalongon to Kawasan Falls in Matutinao, Badian. It takes about
4–6 hours
, and because the trail forks in many places, a local guide is essential. Post-typhoon repair work is ongoing on the Kawasan Falls side, so check whether it is open before you set out.

blocks.title: Walk through the highland vegetable fields

children.text: Walk among Mantalongon's terraced vegetable fields and farmhouses to see daily life in inland rural Cebu. During harvest season, you can buy fresh vegetables cheaply.
At the market in Dalaguete town below the mountain, you can buy highland vegetables, fruit, and local snacks cheaply. The Spanish-era church along the coastal road is also worth a look.

The summit's most open view faces west toward the Tañon Strait, where Moalboal and Badian Island lie. The sun sets over that sea, so the sunset is easier to watch head-on than the sunrise, and many reviews say that in the dry season, when morning mist is common, the sunset is more likely to give a clear view. Sunset falls roughly between
depending on the time of year. It gets dark on the way down, so be sure to bring a headlamp.
Casino Peak (Lugsangan Peak) is about
5 minutes
by car from Osmeña Peak. The entrance fee is about
, and it takes
10–15 minutes

to reach the top, but the slope is steep, so you need non-slip shoes. Rounded green hills roll on one after another, creating a scene that resembles Bohol's Chocolate Hills. It's a good stop to add on during the morning after the sunrise hike.

At Cebu City South Bus Terminal, take a Ceres bus bound for Oslob or Santander and get off in Dalaguete town. It takes about
2 hours 30 minutes–3 hours

Chartering a private vehicle from Moalboal, Oslob, or Cebu City is the most convenient. From Moalboal or Oslob it's about

1 hour 20 minutes

at intervals of

items.title: From the west coast (Moalboal, Badian, Alegria)

children.text: If you're staying in Moalboal or Badian, hiring a motorbike that goes straight up the mountain road without passing through Dalaguete is convenient. From Moalboal to the jump-off takes about
1 hour–1 hour 30 minutes
by vehicle, and according to reviews a round trip by motorbike costs around
, negotiated depending on distance and waiting time. For a dawn departure, agree on the time and fare with the driver the day before.
From Cebu City, take the southern coastal road to Dalaguete, then head about
14km
inland from town to reach Mantalongon. The road is narrow and steep, but ordinary cars can make it, and parking is often donation-based. Renting a scooter in Moalboal or Oslob costs around
a day, but driving the mountain road at dawn or in the rain is recommended only for experienced riders.
The dry season from
December
to
May
is best. During this time, clear skies give good views of the sunrise and distant scenery, and the trail stays dry and non-slippery.
December–February
sees dawn temperatures drop to around 15–18°C, with frequent seas of cloud, while
March–May
turns the grass yellow for a different atmosphere.
During the rainy season,
June–November
, clouds and rain roll in almost every afternoon, obscuring the view on many days, and the clay trail turns to mud. Avoid the traverse during typhoon season (mainly
August–November

). If hiking during the rainy season, an early morning hike, when weather is relatively stable, is recommended. Dawn is much cooler here than on the coast year-round, so bring a light long-sleeve layer.
If you're aiming for the sunrise,
March–May
, with less rain, is the most reliable, though some days morning mist blocks the view, and many reviews say sunset viewing is good in
December–January
. Sunrise falls roughly between

throughout the year, so leaving the jump-off about 1 hour before sunrise is about right. On weekends, especially Sundays and holiday periods, crowds make it hard to claim a spot at the summit, and weekday dawns are much quieter.

Around the Mantalongon jump-off there are a few homestays and simple lodges, running about
a night. For an easy sunrise hike, staying here or camping at the summit is best. Most travelers stay at beach accommodations in Moalboal (about
1 hour 30 minutes
by car) or Oslob (about
1 hour 30 minutes
by car) and set off at dawn.

Small eateries and shops near the jump-off sell simple breakfasts like coffee, instant noodles, and eggs with rice. Soups and stir-fries made from highland-grown vegetables are simple but delicious. Along the Dalaguete coastal road there are Filipino restaurants and bakeries, and you can buy mangoes and other southern Cebu specialty fruit cheaply on the street.
Mantalongon market is busiest at dawn,
4–6 AM

. That's when merchants from the coast come up to buy highland vegetables such as cabbage, carrots, and lettuce, and this area is a major source of the vegetables that go into Cebu's markets. At small eateries around the market you can have breakfast of lugaw (rice porridge) and coffee, and buy vegetables at market prices.

Besides homestays, private campsites and glamping facilities also operate near the summit, but fees and booking methods differ by facility, so it's best to contact them before you set out. If you want to relax at the beach, the most common plan is to stay at Panagsama Beach in Moalboal or in Oslob and come up at dawn. On the way back, you can buy fruit and snacks at Dalaguete town market and the shops along the coastal road.
A headlamp is essential for a sunrise hike. A phone flashlight drains the battery quickly and makes it hard to keep both hands free.
The rocks near the summit are sharp and narrow, so wear sneakers or hiking shoes with good grip.
It's windy and chilly at dawn and at the summit. Bring a windbreaker or a light long-sleeve layer.
At the jump-off, you can pay the entrance fee, register, and be introduced to a guide. If it's your first visit, using a guide for the dawn hike is safer.
Entrance fees, habal-habal, and meals are all cash-only. There's no ATM on the mountain, so prepare change.
Mobile signal is generally available near the summit, but it can drop out along the valley section of the traverse.
To see the sunrise together with a sea of clouds, aim for a clear day in
December–February
, even within the dry season.
Sundays and public holidays are the busiest. If you go at dawn on a weekday, you can comfortably find a spot for photos at the summit.
At sunrise, the sun comes up behind you. Stand with the view toward Moalboal and Badian Island in front of you and photograph the peaks catching the slanting sunlight.
Campfires are prohibited, and camp cooking is done only with portable stoves. The designated trail passes through farmland, so don't stray from it, and fly a drone only after getting permission.
The summit peaks are steep with no railings. Don't step out to the cliff edge for photos.
When it rains, the clay trail becomes very slippery. It's safer to cancel the traverse in wet weather.
The traverse route has many forking paths and it's easy to get lost. Always go with a local guide.
The mountain road from Dalaguete to Mantalongon has many steep grades and sharp curves. Ask for a helmet when riding a habal-habal.
When camping, only build fires in designated spots, and carry all your trash back down.
When a typhoon or tropical storm warning is issued, hiking sites may be temporarily closed. During Tropical Storm Basyang in
February 2026
, Wind Signal No. 2 was raised over Dalaguete, and after Typhoon Tino in
November 2025

, places such as Kawasan Falls in southern Cebu were closed for a while. In bad weather periods, check with the Dalaguete tourism office or a local guide before setting out to see whether the site is open.
Weather on the mountain differs from the coast. Even if it's clear at the coast, the summit can be shrouded in cloud, so keep your expectations flexible.
